state.case_summary:
A 42-year-old man with 30 pack-years of smoking, cannabis use, alcohol dependence, and the use of herbal products for addiction cessation presented with a 3-day history of acute urinary retention, hematemesis, and progressive neurological deficits. On day 3, he developed marked paraparesis of the lower limbs (muscle strength 2/5), was unable to stand or walk, and had hyperreflexia with sustained clonus in the lower extremities. Sensory function—including proprioception, light touch, and vibration—was normal. He also had hypertonic sphincters and hyperalgesia. Cranial nerve and upper limb examinations were normal. He was febrile, and his condition deteriorated into respiratory distress requiring intubation and sedation.

Lumbar puncture revealed clear cerebrospinal fluid without albuminocytologic dissociation: glucose 0.49 g/L, protein 0.20 g/L, chloride 121 mmol/L, 14 white blood cells (70% lymphocytes), and 14 red blood cells per mm³; cultures were sterile. Blood tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL falling to 8.2 g/dL), leukocytosis (18 350 cells/μL), platelet counts fluctuating between 98 000 and 136 000 cells/μL, hyponatremia corrected from 117.5 mEq/L to 146 mEq/L over 8 days, potassium levels between 5.5 and 4.6 mEq/L, elevated AST (134 U/L) and ALT (65.9 U/L), and CRP 128.8–131.2 mg/L. Renal function remained normal.

Initial brain MRI showed multiple bilateral, symmetrical T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the periventricular and periaqueductal regions, dorsomedial thalami, medial temporal lobes, caudate nuclei, and brainstem, with diffusion restriction and low ADC values. Spinal MRI demonstrated diffuse T2 hyperintensities throughout the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar cord. A follow-up MRI a few days later revealed worsening of these lesions, new involvement of the lenticular nuclei, and patchy contrast enhancement in the cerebral peduncles, superior cerebellar peduncles, superior colliculi, right pons, and bilateral medulla. There was more extensive bilateral FLAIR hyperintensity in the medial temporal lobes and periventricular white matter and progression of the spinal cord lesions.

Contrast-enhanced CT showed lymphadenopathy in the bilateral cervical and axillary regions, left inguinal lymphadenopathy, and marked peri- and pararenal soft-tissue infiltration.

root.label: Subacute Progressive Multisystem Syndrome with Neurological Deficits, Constitutional Alarm Signs, and Lymphadenopathy
supporting_facts: Lymphadenopathy in bilateral cervical and axillary regions
excluded_candidates: Infectious aetiology: possibility of CNS infection, but lack of albuminocytologic dissociation and sterile CSF cultures make it less likely
Metabolic disorder: possibility of a metabolic disorder, but normal renal function and lack of other specific findings make it less likely
Autoimmune disorder: possibility of an autoimmune disorder, but lack of specific antibodies and normal CSF findings make it less likely
